fixes.explanation: A good guess, friend, since battles show up in a lot of stories. But this verse names a different blessing: "…the blessing of life forevermore." (Psalm 133:3). Battles don't come up in this psalm at all. It's all oil, dew and brothers together.

A great name sounds like a fine blessing, so I get the guess. But the verse says the LORD bestowed "…the blessing of life forevermore." (Psalm 133:3). Nothing about a name is mentioned there. Life forevermore is the blessing on the table.

Watching the gate is a fine job, but it's not in this verse. The song calls out, "Come, bless the LORD, all you servants of the LORD who serve by night in the house of the LORD!" (Psalm 134:1). The call is to bless the LORD. Gates aren't mentioned.

I see the thinking, friend, since a king sounds like someone who would hand out blessings. But the last line of Psalm 134 doesn't name a king. It says, "May the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth, bless you from Zion." (Psalm 134:3). The blessing comes from the LORD.

Yes, friend. "May the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth, bless you from Zion." (Psalm 134:3). The Maker of heaven and earth is the One doing the blessing from there. Zion was also where the dew fell in David's picture (Psalm 133:3). Two songs, one place.

Bethel is a fine name to guess, but it isn't in this song. The last line says, "May the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth, bless you from Zion." (Psalm 134:3). Zion is the place named. Zion also appears in the song before this one (Psalm 133:3).

Sinai is a big name, and I get why it came to mind. But this song says, "May the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth, bless you from Zion." (Psalm 134:3). Zion is the place named here. It's the same Zion from the dew in the song before it (Psalm 133:3).
